title: Ownership and Moves
summary: The three ownership rules, the stack and the heap, how String owns heap memory and frees it when dropped, moves versus copies, the Copy trait for simple values, clone for explicit deep copies, ownership through function calls and return values, and why this replaces both garbage collection and manual free.

cards.q: When is a `String`'s heap memory freed?
cards.a:
When its owner goes out of scope, unless it was moved elsewhere first

The owner drops the value at the end of its scope; if ownership moved (to another variable or a function), the new owner frees it instead. Rust has no garbage collector.

cards.q: Why can you still use `a` after `let b = a;` when `a` is an `i32` but not when it is a `String`?
cards.a:
`i32` is `Copy`, so it is copied; a `String` owns heap data, so it is moved

Copying an `i32` is trivial and safe; two owners of one `String` buffer would both free it, so the `String` moves and `a` becomes unusable. A deep copy needs an explicit `.clone()`.

cards.q: After `let v = vec![1, 2]; let w = v;`, which is true?
cards.a:
The vector moved to `w` and `v` can no longer be used

`Vec` owns heap memory, so assignment moves it; the code compiles as long as `v` is not used afterwards.
